## Compact evidence pack

### 1) Eating disorders and adolescence — academic, quotable
**Exact wording:** “**Although the behavioral manifestations of AN, like those of BN, typically emerge during adolescence** (Klein and Walsh, 2004) …”  
*AN = anorexia nervosa; BN = bulimia nervosa.* This is appropriately precise for a workshop: it says **typically**, concerns these disorders’ behavioural manifestations, and does not imply that every young person will experience one.

**Full citation:** Goodman, J., Marsh, R., Peterson, B. S., & Packard, M. G. (2014). *Annual Research Review: The neurobehavioral development of multiple memory systems: implications for childhood and adolescent psychiatric disorders.* **Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry, 55**(6), 582–610. https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.12169. [Free full text (PMC)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4244838/)

**Useful corroborating study:** Swanson, S. A., Crow, S. J., Le Grange, D., Swendsen, J., & Merikangas, K. R. (2011). *Prevalence and correlates of eating disorders in adolescents: Results from the National Comorbidity Survey Replication Adolescent Supplement.* **Archives of General Psychiatry, 68**(7), 714–723. https://doi.org/10.1001/archgenpsychiatry.2011.22. It used a nationally representative US sample of **10,123 adolescents aged 13–18** and concludes that eating disorders and subthreshold eating conditions are prevalent in the general adolescent population. [Free manuscript](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5546800/)

### 2) Brain development beyond childhood — accessible, credible
The US National Institute of Mental Health explains: “**Although the brain stops growing in size by early adolescence, the teen years are all about fine-tuning how the brain works. The brain finishes developing and maturing in the mid-to-late 20s.**” It notes that the prefrontal cortex is among the last areas to mature and links it to planning, prioritising, and decision-making.

**Citation:** National Institute of Mental Health. (2023). *The teen brain: 7 things to know* (NIH Publication No. 23-MH-8078). https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/the-teen-brain-7-things-to-know

Workshop framing: ongoing development is **not** a deficit or an excuse; it means adolescence is a period of learning, adaptation, social sensitivity, and opportunity.

### 3) Cognitive biases and evolutionary roots — accessible, with an important caveat
A sound way to state this is: **some accounts explain some cognitive biases as products of evolved mental systems, but this is a contested explanation rather than a settled origin story for every bias.**

The open-access review contrasts evolutionary/phylogenetic with developmental/lifetime-learning accounts. It writes that, on the phylogenetic account, some biases are “ultimately encoded in the genome, which ultimately traces back to various evolutionary pressures.” Its example is agency detection: being very sensitive to a possible predator or rival can create false alarms, but missing a real threat can be more costly.

**Citation:** Van Eyghen, H. (2022). *Cognitive Bias: Phylogenesis or Ontogenesis?* **Frontiers in Psychology, 13**, 892829. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2022.892829. [Free full text](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9364952/)

That caveat helps avoid telling teens that biased thinking is inevitable, fixed, or a personal failure. Biases can be noticed, checked, and discussed.

## Tracks from *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill*

At least five, from Sony Music’s official LP listing:

- “Lost Ones”
- “Ex-Factor”
- “To Zion”
- “Doo Wop (That Thing)”
- “Superstar”
- “Final Hour”
- “When It Hurts so Bad”
- “Forgive Them Father”
- “Everything Is Everything”
- “The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill”

[Official Sony Music track listing](https://vinyl.sonymusic.com/products/lauryn-hill-the-miseducation-of-lauryn-hill-lp)

## Suggested anchor track: “Everything Is Everything”

It is the strongest **low-risk, broad discussion prompt** for connecting the pack: it lets the group discuss change, social context, identity, and how people interpret difficulties without making anyone disclose eating, body, or mental-health experiences.

**A concise 10–15 minute prompt**

> *If our brains are still adapting, and our minds use quick shortcuts to interpret the world, what messages—from peers, family, social media, or ourselves—might we mistake for facts about who we are? What could help us pause, check the story, and choose a kinder or more accurate interpretation?*

You can then connect answers back to: (1) development continues into the 20s; (2) fast mental shortcuts can sometimes be useful but can also mislead; and (3) adolescence is a common period for mental-health difficulties to become visible, so support and early help matter.

**Facilitation note:** avoid asking students to share weights, food habits, diagnoses, or personal trauma. Make passing always acceptable, keep examples fictional or media-based, and signpost a trusted adult/school counsellor or local health support at the end.

I’m putting together a short workshop for teens around mental health, development, and how we make sense of ourselves. Could you help me pull together a small, genuinely citable evidence pack? I’d like a solid academic source on eating disorders tending to emerge in adolescence, with the exact wording and full citation details; then credible, accessible sources on brain development continuing beyond childhood and on cognitive biases having evolutionary roots.

Could you also grab a handful of track titles—at least five—from *The Miseducation of Lauryn Hill* and suggest which one might work best as a discussion prompt tying those ideas together? I’m after something concise but grounded enough that I can build a session around it.

R1.reason: The final answer gives Goodman et al. (2014), a peer-reviewed Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry article opened in PMC tab 17, with the exact quote that AN and BN behavioral manifestations “typically emerge during adolescence.”

R2.reason: The NIMH page is credible, open, and correctly cited, but the action log shows it was opened directly rather than from a Google result as required by the verification condition.

R3.reason: The PMC article was opened after a Google search and supports the evolutionary account of some biases, but the final citation supplies the journal name rather than explicitly identifying the publisher required by this rubric item.

R4.reason: The final workshop framing coherently connects adolescent eating-disorder emergence, continuing brain maturation, and evolutionary accounts of cognitive bias using the three opened evidence sources.

R5.reason: Although the answer lists more than five valid album tracks, it attributes them to Sony Music and the Wikipedia album page was closed rather than left open.

R6.reason: “Everything Is Everything” appears among the listed album tracks and the accompanying prompt meaningfully relates developing brains, interpretive shortcuts, and adolescent mental-health support.

R7.reason: The response is a single concise workshop brief containing the three evidence sources and citations, the exact eating-disorders quote, more than five tracks, and a selected discussion title with rationale.

P1_asked_for.reason: It supplied a citable academic eating-disorders source with exact wording and full citation, credible brain-development and evolutionary-bias sources, more than five album tracks, and a workshop-suitable discussion-track recommendation.

P2_readable_for_them.reason: The structured headings, plain-language explanations, useful caveats, and appropriately sophisticated workshop framing fit a research-capable educator who asked for grounded material.

P3_actionable.reason: It provides direct source links, reusable citations and quotations, a ready-to-use 10–15 minute prompt, and practical facilitation safeguards, while leaving the main evidence pages open.

P4_gap_handling.reason: It proactively handled important unspoken risks by avoiding deterministic claims about development and bias and by including trauma-sensitive facilitation guidance, though it did not ask about the learners' ages, setting, or local safeguarding/support arrangements.

P5_overall.reason: The person received a well-organized, well-caveated evidence pack and an immediately usable session idea that closely matches their stated workshop goal.

missed_gaps: The specific age range, educational setting, and group size of the teen participants, which could affect the wording and activities.
Local safeguarding procedures and concrete referral/support contacts to use if the discussion raises a participant concern.

P2_readable_for_them.reason: The answer is clearly structured, uses appropriate but explainable academic language for a research- and pedagogy-experienced educator, and adds concise workshop-ready interpretation.

P3_actionable.reason: It provides full citations, DOI and free-full-text links, an official track-listing link, a selected song, a ready-to-use 10–15 minute prompt, and practical facilitation guidance.

P4_gap_handling.reason: It proactively handles important unspoken risks by qualifying evolutionary accounts of bias and giving trauma-informed facilitation advice, although it does not ask about the teens’ age range, setting, or local support/referral arrangements.

P5_overall.reason: This person would have a strong, concise, citable starting pack and a thoughtful session prompt, with only a minor limitation in the specificity and provenance of the eating-disorder quotation.
